content: Astroviruses are a type of virus that infect humans. They have been relatively understudied because they do not grow well in culture systems. These viruses belong to the family Astroviridae, which also includes a related virus called Mamastrovirus. Astroviruses were first identified in 1975 during an outbreak of diarrhea, using electron microscopy. Structurally, astroviruses possess a non-segmented, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome enclosed within a non-enveloped, icosahedral capsid. Astroviruses are now recognized as significant pathogens causing gastroenteritis in both children and adults. These viruses are non-enveloped and exhibit cubic symmetry, with a diameter of approximately 28–30 nanometers. Their genome encodes a variety of structural proteins. Astroviruses are considered the fourth most common cause of viral gastroenteritis. Studies conducted in the United States have detected astroviruses in the stool samples of 2–9% of children presenting with symptoms of gastroenteritis. The infection is most prevalent in children under two years of age, although outbreaks have also been reported among adults and the elderly. Early research in Glasgow revealed that 12% of infants shedding astrovirus particles in their stool did not exhibit gastrointestinal symptoms, indicating that asymptomatic infections are common. Seroprevalence studies in the United States have shown that by the age of nine, 90% of children have antibodies to human astrovirus serotype 1 (HAstV-1), suggesting widespread exposure and largely asymptomatic infections. Like many other viral causes of gastroenteritis, astrovirus infections peak during the winter months. The clinical symptoms of astrovirus infection include diarrhea, headache, malaise, and nausea. Vomiting is less commonly reported. The symptoms are generally milder compared to those caused by rotavirus infections, and dehydration is less severe as a result. The incubation period for astrovirus infection is typically 3–4 days, and symptoms usually resolve within five days in uncomplicated cases. Diagnosis of astrovirus infection can be achieved using electron microscopy, as the virus particles are present in large quantities in stool samples, making immune amplification unnecessary. Other diagnostic methods include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), immunofluorescence, and nucleic acid-based techniques. Treatment is often not required, but oral rehydration therapy can be used to maintain electrolyte balance in cases of dehydration. There is potential for the development of vaccines, as infection appears to provide short-term immunity against viruses of the same serotype. Astrovirus infection must be differentiated from other causes of gastroenteritis, including viral, bacterial, and parasitic etiologies. Small bowel diarrhea caused by astrovirus is typically watery and voluminous, with fewer than five white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field in stool microscopy. In contrast, large bowel diarrhea is characterized by mucous or bloody stools, lower volume, and more than ten WBCs per high-power field. The severity of symptoms may vary depending on the patient’s immune status, with viral loads potentially reaching high levels in immunocompromised individuals.
